title: Ordering coffee in New York
setting: It's 8 a.m. at a busy coffee shop in Manhattan, New York. The line moves fast, the barista is friendly but quick, and everyone seems to know exactly what they want.
objectives: Order a drink the way Americans usually do
Understand quick questions like "Room for milk?" and "For here or to go?"
Know what to do when the screen asks for a tip
varietyNote: This is everyday American English, as you'd hear it in New York. British English uses some different phrases for the same things — "to take away" instead of "to go", for example (see the London adventure). American English itself varies by region, but the phrases here are understood everywhere in the US.

phrases.text: Can I get a medium iced coffee, please?
phrases.translation: I'd like a medium iced coffee, please.
phrases.example: Hi! Can I get a large latte and a blueberry muffin?
phrases.exampleTranslation: Hello! I'd like a large latte and a blueberry muffin.
phrases.note: "Can I get…?" is the normal, polite way to order in the US. It isn't rude — it's what almost everyone says.

alsoHeard.text: I'll have a medium iced coffee.
alsoHeard.where: Also very common in the US

alsoHeard.text: Could I have a medium iced coffee?
alsoHeard.where: A little more formal; common in the UK too

phrases.translation: Should I leave space at the top so you can add milk?
phrases.exampleTranslation: The barista asks whether to leave space in the cup.

phrases.translation: Will you drink it here, or take it with you?
phrases.exampleTranslation: I'll take it with me, please.
"Do you want anything else?" "No, thank you."
phrases.note: Here "I'm good" doesn't describe how you feel — it means you don't need anything more.

phrases.text: What name should I put on it?
phrases.translation: What's your name? (so we can call you when your drink is ready)
phrases.exampleTranslation: Another common way to ask for your name.
A friendly way to say goodbye.

cultureNotes: In a busy New York coffee shop, short and friendly is the norm. Ordering quickly isn't rude — holding up the line is what people notice.
The card screen often suggests a tip. Tipping at a counter is common but optional; a small tip or a dollar is typical, and "No tip" is always an option.
Cup sizes vary by chain: small, medium and large in most places, but other names at some big chains.
"How are you?" from staff is a greeting, not a real question. "Good, thanks — how are you?" is all you need.

steps.text: You reach the front of the line. The barista smiles.

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.text: Hi there! What can I get you?

steps.prompt: You'd like a medium iced coffee. How do you order it?

options.text: Can I get a medium iced coffee, please?
options.why: Natural, polite and exactly how people order in the US.

options.text: Give me a coffee medium iced.
options.why: The word order is off ("a medium iced coffee"), and "Give me…" without "please" sounds demanding.

options.text: I would like to receive one coffee with ice in the medium size.
options.why: Grammatically fine, but it sounds like a textbook — very stiff for a fast coffee line.

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.translation: Of course. Should I leave space for milk?

options.text: Whether to leave space at the top of the cup for milk
options.why: Right — "room" here means space, not a room in a building.

options.text: Whether you'd like to sit in the room with the milk
options.why: "Room" can mean a room, but here it means space in the cup.

options.text: Whether you want milk instead of coffee
options.why: You'd still get coffee — this is only about leaving space to add milk yourself.

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.translation: Will you drink it here or take it with you?

steps.prompt: You're taking it to the office. What do you say?

options.why: "To go" is the fixed American expression for taking food or drinks away.
Understandable, but it isn't the expression people use — say "to go".
That's British English. You'll be understood, but in New York people say "to go".

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.text: Anything else? The muffins just came out of the oven.
steps.translation: Do you want anything else? The muffins are fresh.

steps.prompt: You don't want anything else. How do you say no, politely and naturally?

options.why: The casual American way to say "no thanks" to an offer.
Clear, but on its own it sounds curt. Add "thanks" — or say "I'm good, thanks".
That answers "How are you?", not an offer of muffins — it may confuse the barista.

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.text: That's $4.75. What name should I put on it?
steps.translation: It costs $4.75. What's your name, for the order?

steps.text: You give your name and tap your card. The screen shows: 15% · 20% · 25% · Custom · No tip.

steps.prompt: What should you do about the tip screen?

options.text: Tipping at a counter is common but optional — a small tip is typical, and "No tip" is fine too.
options.why: Right. Counter tips are appreciated, not required. Sit-down restaurants are different: there, 15–20% is expected.

options.text: You must choose at least 20% — anything less is against the law.
options.why: Tips are never required by law. At a counter it's entirely your choice.

options.text: Always press "No tip" — tipping is considered rude in the US.
options.why: It isn't rude at all. Many people leave a small tip for counter service.

steps.speaker: Barista
steps.translation: Thank you! Have a good day!

steps.prompt: What does "Have a good one!" mean?

options.why: A casual, friendly goodbye. You can answer "You too!".
Close in spirit, but "one" means your day (or evening), not the coffee.
It's just a goodbye, not an invitation to buy another.
